evidence.quote: A spring freshet of unusual volume had flooded the adjacent river until, bursting its bounds, it escaped through the narrow, wedge-shaped valley that held Redwood Camp. For a day and night the surcharged river poured half its waters through the straggling camp. At the end of that time every vestige of the little settlement was swept away
evidence.paraphrase: A massive flood destroys Redwood Camp entirely.

evidence.quote: one fragment--bearing up Elijah Martin--pursuing the devious courses of an unknown tributary fifty miles away
evidence.paraphrase: The protagonist is carried fifty miles away by the flood to an unknown place.

evidence.quote: Eventually he was caught in a side current, swept to the bank, and cast ashore on an unexplored wilderness.
evidence.paraphrase: He ends up stranded in an unexplored wilderness away from his former surroundings.

evidence.quote: It was a "sweathouse," an institution common to nearly all the aboriginal tribes of California. Half a religious temple, it was also half a sanitary asylum, was used as a Russian bath or superheated vault, from which the braves, sweltering and stifling all night, by smothered fires, at early dawn plunged, perspiring, into the ice-cold river.
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator explains the function and cultural use of an Indian sweathouse.

evidence.quote: their medicine-men had prophesied that his perfect successor should appear miraculously before them, borne noiselessly on the river FROM THE SEA, in the plumes and insignia of his predecessor
evidence.paraphrase: The tribe's prophecy causes them to accept the stranded outcast as their supernatural new chief.

evidence.quote: it must be confessed that, in spite of the cherished theories of most romances and all statesmen and commanders, that FEAR is the great civilizer of the savage barbarian, and that he is supposed to regard the prowess of the white man and his mysterious death-dealing weapons as evidence of his supernatural origin and superior creation, the facts have generally pointed to the reverse
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator contrasts common assumptions about how natives view white power with what he claims are the actual facts.

evidence.quote: He only saw that he, hitherto ignored and despised in a community of half-barbaric men, now translated to a community of men wholly savage, was respected and worshipped!
evidence.paraphrase: Elijah realizes that he is now respected and worshipped rather than despised.

evidence.quote: The sudden conflict and utter revulsion of emotion that those simple words caused in Elijah's breast was almost incredible.
evidence.paraphrase: Hearing himself praised as a born king causes a profound emotional transformation in Elijah.

evidence.quote: it was presently announced throughout the frontier settlements that the hitherto insignificant and peaceful tribe of Minyos, who inhabited a large territory bordering on the Pacific Ocean, had developed into a powerful nation, only kept from the war-path by a more powerful but mysterious chief
evidence.paraphrase: As a result of Elijah's leadership, the tribe's reputation and status change dramatically across the frontier.

evidence.quote: They waxed prosperous and rich; they lost their nomadic habits--a centralized settlement bearing the external signs of an Indian village took the place of their old temporary encampments
evidence.paraphrase: Under Elijah's rule the tribe becomes prosperous and shifts from nomadic to settled life.

evidence.quote: Elijah Martin, foundling, outcast, without civilized ties or relationship of any kind, forgotten by his countrymen, and lifted into alien power, wealth, security, and respect, became--homesick!
evidence.paraphrase: Despite his new power and wealth, Elijah becomes homesick.

evidence.quote: an outrage--so atrocious that even the peaceful Minyos were thrilled with savage indignation--was committed on the outskirts of the village. An old chief, who had been specially selected to deal with the Indian agent, and who kept a small trading outpost, had been killed and his goods despoiled by a reckless Redwood packer.
evidence.paraphrase: A packer murders an old chief, triggering a demand for vengeance.

evidence.quote: he knew the impersonal character of Indian retribution and compensation--a sacrifice of equal value, without reference to the culpability of the victim
evidence.paraphrase: The narrator explains the Minyo custom of vicarious retribution, where any equivalent life may be taken in compensation.

evidence.quote: "HIS squaw!" He staggered back. A terrible suspicion flashed upon him. He dashed Wachita aside and ran to the tree. It was the body of the Indian agent!
evidence.paraphrase: Elijah discovers with horror that the killed captive was the Indian agent, not the murderer.

evidence.quote: "So the Gov'rment hev at last woke up and wiped out them cussed Digger Minyos," said Snapshot Harry, as he laid down the newspaper
evidence.paraphrase: The government destroys and relocates the Minyo tribe following the agent's death.

evidence.quote: "Why, you might as well hev suspected HIM of being the big chief himself!"
evidence.paraphrase: The men mock the idea that the despised Skeesicks could have been the great chief, which the reader knows to be true.
